Mutating the `pr` variable declared in the outer scope is not safe when the re-poll throws
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**Mutating the `pr` variable declared in the outer scope is not safe when the re-poll throws**

On a re-poll failure the catch block logs and falls through, leaving `pr` at whatever value it held before — which is the stale pre-cycle snapshot, not the post-first-provider body. That is the correct degraded behavior, and the log message says so. However `pr` was declared with `let` in the outer scope and is also used for the merged/closed guard at the top of the loop. If a re-poll failure happens mid-cycle and then the loop continues to the next cycle, the outer `pr` is still the refreshed value from the last *successful* re-poll (or the original poll at cycle start). This is not a bug in the current single-cycle test scenario but could produce unexpected skips in multi-cycle production runs where `pr.head.sha` from a mid-cycle refresh differs from the next cycle's actual poll result.

The real fix is to scope the mid-cycle refresh to a local variable rather than reassigning the outer `pr`:
```ts
const refreshed = await pollOctokit.request(...);
pr = refreshed.data; // ← this mutates the outer loop variable
```
Consider assigning to a local `let currentPr` used only within the target loop, keeping `pr` as the cycle-start snapshot.

claims.title: Re-poll catch block continues silently; the next target receives the stale body with no indication of why
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Re-poll catch block continues silently; the next target receives the stale body with no indication of why**

When the re-poll after a provider's post fails, the catch block logs a warning (good), but `pr` is left pointing at the stale pre-cycle snapshot. The warning message explains the consequence (`next provider's PR-body PATCH may overwrite it`) but the next target's `submitReview` call then silently overwrites the first provider's PR-body section with no further indication that this is happening. This is acceptable as a best-effort fallback, but the log message should include the current `targetIndex` / provider name so it's actionable in production logs — the current message omits which provider just posted.

claims.title: `hasExistingComment` fetches only the first page of comments
`rateLimitCommentMarker` uses `config.provider` but `quotaCommentMarker` uses `review.quotaProvider` — inconsistency may cause missed dedup
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**`rateLimitCommentMarker` uses `config.provider` but `quotaCommentMarker` uses `review.quotaProvider` — inconsistency may cause missed dedup**

For the rate-limit path, the marker is keyed on `config.provider` (the currently configured provider). For the quota path, it is keyed on `review.quotaProvider` (the provider that reported the exhaustion). These can differ when `config.provider` is `"auto"` or a meta-provider that delegates. If the two callers disagree on the provider string used to build the marker, `hasExistingComment` will search for a marker that was never written (or vice-versa), defeating the dedup. This should be verified and, if they can diverge, normalized to one source of truth.

claims.title: Comment claims `lastReviewedSha` would trip the skip guard, but the guard checks `state.lastReviewedSha`, not the persisted value
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Comment claims `lastReviewedSha` would trip the skip guard, but the guard checks `state.lastReviewedSha`, not the persisted value**

The comment says:

> Setting the SHA here too would trip the per-target loop's own `pr.head.sha === state.lastReviewedSha` skip guard below and silently skip calling submitReview at all.

This is accurate — `state.lastReviewedSha` is the in-memory value on the `providerState` map entry, so setting it here would cause the guard `if (!state || pr.head.sha === state.lastReviewedSha) continue;` to fire and skip the call entirely. The comment is correct. However, the phrase "silently skip" could mislead a maintainer into thinking this is always undesirable: in a fresh (non-restart) session this skip is exactly the right behavior. Tightening the wording to "silently skip calling submitReview *on cycle 1*, before buildReview's own idempotency check has had a chance to run" would make the intent clearer.

claims.title: Test asserts `request` called twice but the first call is the initial poll — the assertion is fragile if poll retry logic is ever added
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Test asserts `request` called twice but the first call is the initial poll — the assertion is fragile if poll retry logic is ever added**

The test `re-polls the PR before the next target's post` uses `mockResolvedValueOnce` for two sequential `request` calls and then asserts `expect(request).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2)`. This correctly covers the happy path. However, the assertion will silently pass even if the re-poll is accidentally called a third time (it would return `undefined` on a third call, potentially throwing). Consider adding an upper-bound check or using `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2)` as a strict count — which it already does. The real risk is that `mockResolvedValue` (not `Once`) is used as the fallback, so a third unexpected call would resolve to the last `pollResponse` rather than failing loudly. This makes the test less able to catch regressions where an extra poll is introduced. Not a bug in the fix itself, but a test robustness gap.

**Pagination termination test only verifies call count, not that no warning was posted**

claims.title: Per-page constant used both as page size and as the 'has-next-page' threshold — a full page of exactly 100 comments would be misread as 'more pages exist' when it is the last page
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Per-page constant used both as page size and as the 'has-next-page' threshold — a full page of exactly 100 comments would be misread as 'more pages exist' when it is the last page**

The loop exits early when `comments.length < HAS_EXISTING_COMMENT_PER_PAGE`. GitHub returns exactly `per_page` items on every full page, including the last one when the total count is a multiple of `per_page`. If a PR has exactly 100, 200, … 1000 comments and none contain the marker, the loop will make one extra request that returns an empty array before terminating — that extra request is harmless and the function still returns `false` correctly. However, if a PR has exactly 100 comments and the 100th comment contains the marker, the loop finds it on page 1 and returns `true` correctly. So the only genuine edge-case is a wasted request when `total % 100 === 0` and no marker exists, which is minor. More importantly, the current termination condition is the standard paginate-until-short-page idiom used by GitHub's own SDKs, so no fix is required — but the comment in the docstring ('a page returns fewer than that') would be clearer if it noted the empty-page case for the exact-multiple scenario.

claims.title: Pagination termination condition uses response length, not a Link header — may stop one page early if GitHub returns exactly 100 on the last page
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Pagination termination condition uses response length, not a Link header — may stop one page early if GitHub returns exactly 100 on the last page**

The loop breaks when `comments.length < HAS_EXISTING_COMMENT_PER_PAGE`. If GitHub returns exactly 100 comments on the true last page (i.e. total comments is a multiple of 100), the loop will fetch one more page, get an empty array, and then correctly return `false` — so in that edge case it makes one extra request, which is acceptable. However, if the last page returns exactly 100 comments *and* the marker is not among them, the loop continues to page+1 which returns an empty array (length 0 < 100), and returns false correctly. This is fine. But if total comments is exactly a multiple of 100 and the marker is not present, the extra empty-page request is wasted. This is a minor efficiency concern, not a correctness bug — the existing logic is safe. No action required unless API rate usage is a concern.

claims.title: Test for `loadPersistedState` KV failure doesn't assert the log message content is observable — passes even if `log` is never called
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**Test for `loadPersistedState` KV failure doesn't assert the log message content is observable — passes even if `log` is never called**

The test at line ~612 of watch.test.ts calls `expect(log).toHaveBeenCalledWith(expect.stringContaining("loadPersistedState unavailable"))`. This assertion is correct and will fail if the log is not called. However, the test does not pass a `loadPersistedState` injectable that actually throws — it relies on the *default* implementation constructing a real KV client and failing. If `createUpstashKv()` in the test environment doesn't throw (e.g. because env vars happen to be set in CI), the test passes but the log line being tested is never exercised. The test would be more reliable if it directly tested the `loadPersistedState` path with an injectable that throws, rather than relying on environment-driven KV construction failure.

claims.title: GET comment body typed as unknown — narrowing to `{ body?: string | null }` relies on unchecked cast
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**GET comment body typed as unknown — narrowing to `{ body?: string | null }` relies on unchecked cast**

The cast `existing.data as Array<{ body?: string | null }>` is made without checking the element type, only the outer array. If GitHub ever returns an array of non-object items (e.g. the paginated list API changes shape), `c.body` would be `undefined` and the `includes` check would silently return false. This is low-risk in practice but the cast discards the type information that Octokit's generated types already provide. Using the Octokit-typed response directly (or at least checking `c != null && typeof c === 'object'` before accessing `.body`) would be safer than the bare cast.

claims.text:

**Test assertion counts list calls but does not assert `per_page` or `page` params are passed correctly**

The test `"stops paginating once a page returns fewer than per_page comments"` asserts `listCalls.toHaveLength(2)` but does not verify that `per_page: 100` and `page: 1` / `page: 2` were actually passed in each call. A refactor that drops the `per_page` or `page` params would still pass this test while breaking the pagination contract. Adding `expect(listCalls[0].params).toMatchObject({ per_page: 100, page: 1 })` would catch that regression. Criticality: 4.

claims.title: Pagination stop condition counts non-array response as a full page
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Pagination stop condition counts non-array response as a full page**

When `existing.data` is not an array, `comments` is set to `[]` (length 0), which is less than `HAS_EXISTING_COMMENT_PER_PAGE` (100), so the loop correctly terminates and returns `false`. That part is fine.

However, if the API returns a non-array on page 2 (after a full page 1), the loop exits without having scanned all comments. The docstring says a non-array response is treated as "no existing comment", but silently abandoning mid-pagination is subtly different from "non-array on page 1 means nothing found". This is a low-severity gap — in practice the API always returns an array — but the comment and the behaviour don't fully agree.

claims.text:

The test verifies that `listCalls` has length 2, confirming two GETs are issued, but it does not assert that each call includes `per_page: 100`. If `hasExistingComment` were accidentally changed to omit `per_page` (reverting to GitHub's default of 30), the test would still pass because the mock ignores the parameter. A per_page assertion would lock in the pagination contract.


The test mock gates page 2 content on `params.page === 2`, which implicitly verifies that `hasExistingComment` actually passes `page` in the request params. This is the right thing to test, but the assertion is entirely inside the mock — if `hasExistingComment` somehow passed `page: undefined` for every call, the mock would always return `page1` (100 items), loop again, and never reach the `listCalls.toHaveLength(2)` expectation correctly. Consider adding a direct assertion on the `page` param of the second list call to make the contract explicit:
```

```
Nit-level: the test still provides meaningful coverage as-is, but the implicit assertion could mask a regression if the loop termination logic changes.

claims.title: Stop condition for pagination uses array length instead of response headers — may over-fetch or under-fetch
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Stop condition for pagination uses array length instead of response headers — may over-fetch or under-fetch**

The loop terminates when `comments.length < HAS_EXISTING_COMMENT_PER_PAGE`. This is the standard heuristic but it has one failure mode visible in the new tests: when a page returns exactly 100 comments and there are no further pages, the loop will make one extra request and get an empty array back (length 0 < 100), which correctly returns `false`. That extra round-trip is harmless, but if a future GitHub API change returns a differently-sized page for the last page (e.g. due to server-side filtering), the heuristic may terminate early or over-fetch. More importantly, the new test `stops paginating once a page returns fewer than per_page comments` passes page2 with 1 comment, but does **not** assert that page 3 is never requested — it only asserts `listCalls.toHaveLength(2)`. If the implementation had a bug where it fetched page 3 anyway, the test would still pass if page 3 also returned something. The test is actually correct as written (two list calls = pages 1 and 2, which is the right behaviour), but the assertion does not prove the *absence* of a page-3 request — it proves there were exactly 2 list calls total, which is sufficient. No code change needed, but the comment in the test body ('`< per_page(100) — no page 3`') overstates what the assertion checks.

After the fix, `marker = quotaCommentMarker(config.provider)` while `billing = billingUrl(quotaProvider)` and the comment body still interpolates `quotaProvider` for the human-facing label. This is intentional per the inline comment, but the variable `quotaProvider` is now doing double duty: it drives the human-readable message AND was previously driving the dedup key. If a future reader sees `quotaProvider` used in the body string and assumes it also controls the marker key, they may re-introduce the bug. Consider a short rename (`displayProvider` / `markerProvider`) or a brief inline note at the `billing` line pointing to the marker's intentional divergence, so the two uses of `quotaProvider` don't look like they should be unified.

claims.title: Docstring claims non-array responses are treated as 'no existing comment' but network errors still propagate
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**Docstring claims non-array responses are treated as 'no existing comment' but network errors still propagate**

The existing comment (carried forward from the original implementation) states that "a malformed or unexpected (non-array) response is treated as 'no existing comment' rather than thrown". This is still accurate for non-array `.data` values. However, a network-level error or an Octokit rejection — which throws before `.data` is accessed — will propagate out of the `for` loop and reject `hasExistingComment`, ultimately rejecting `maybeSubmitReview`. The documented guarantee ('not a hard dependency of the review itself') is not upheld for request-level failures. The prior review already flagged this; the pagination rewrite was applied in this diff but the try/catch fix was not. The comment should either be corrected to reflect actual behavior, or a try/catch should be added around the `octokit.request` call inside the loop and the comment left accurate.

**Pagination stop condition counts non-array response as a full page, suppressing further pages**

When `existing.data` is not an array, `comments` is set to `[]` (length 0). That length is less than `HAS_EXISTING_COMMENT_PER_PAGE`, so the loop returns `false` early — as if the last page was reached — even though the response was malformed. This means a corrupted page in the middle of a paginated result silently aborts the scan and returns `false`, potentially missing an existing marker comment and allowing a duplicate to be posted.

This was already filed as an open finding; raising here only because the wrapping `try/catch` added in this diff does not fix the inner early-exit logic.

claims.title: Per-provider marker function is not exported but callers in other files need it for migration
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**Per-provider marker function is not exported but callers in other files need it for migration**

`prSectionMarkers` is a module-private function introduced to fix the shared-marker bug, yet `injectPRSection` and `buildPRSummarySection` are both exported — meaning callers in other files that previously built their own `PR_SECTION_START`/`PR_SECTION_END` strings (e.g. for searching existing PR bodies on legacy data) now have no way to reconstruct those old markers for a one-time migration. If any production PR body still contains the old unscoped markers `<!-- ai-review-bot:start -->`/`<!-- ai-review-bot:end -->`, `injectPRSection` will append a new provider-scoped section rather than replacing it, leaving both the stale generic block and the new one in the body permanently. This is a silent data-quality regression on any PR touched before this deploy, not a theoretical concern.

claims.title: Old unscoped markers silently accumulate in PR bodies after deploy
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**Old unscoped markers silently accumulate in PR bodies after deploy**

The regex/string search in `injectPRSection` is now provider-scoped, so an existing PR body containing `<!-- ai-review-bot:start -->` and `<!-- ai-review-bot:end -->` (written by any version before this fix) will never match the new `<!-- ai-review-bot:anthropic:start -->` pattern. Subsequent `PATCH` calls will append a fresh provider-scoped section while the legacy generic block remains, producing two copies of the summary in the PR description with no automated cleanup path.

claims.title: Log message still misstates the consequence after per-provider markers landed
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Log message still misstates the consequence after per-provider markers landed**

The updated log message says `"next provider's PR-body PATCH will likely overwrite the just-posted section"`, but with per-provider markers now in place (the real fix for ai-review-bot-1f5), the second provider's PATCH will overwrite an older version of *this* provider's section only if the body it reads predates the just-posted section — it will not overwrite the *other* provider's section at all. The message overstates the blast radius and will mislead whoever triages this warning in production, making them think both providers' sections are at risk when only one is.

*Suggested fix:*

```suggestion
log(
	`ai-review watch: re-poll after ${target.provider} post failed; next provider's PATCH will build on a stale body and may overwrite ${target.provider}'s just-posted section: ${errMsg(pollErr)}`,
);
```

claims.title: Comment on the stale-body risk is now slightly inaccurate after provider-scoped markers
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Comment on the stale-body risk is now slightly inaccurate after provider-scoped markers**

The inline comment at the re-poll site says `"a stale snapshot still risks the next provider's PATCH writing an outright older version of THIS provider's section"`. This is accurate, but the comment three lines above it (removed in the diff, replaced by the current text) still frames the risk as the next provider overwriting this one's section. With provider-scoped markers, the only remaining risk is this provider's own section being rolled back to a pre-post version — not the other provider's section being clobbered. The current comment text (`injectPRSection now uses per-provider markers … a stale snapshot still risks …`) is correct, but the final clause `"so the re-poll is still worth doing on top of that fix, not made redundant by it"` is subtly misleading: the re-poll guards against rolling back *this* provider's own section, not against cross-provider overwrite. Suggest tightening to make that clear.

claims.title: Exact-body match in hasExistingComment is O(N×M) for large comments and may silently fail on trimmed/normalised bodies
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Exact-body match in hasExistingComment is O(N×M) for large comments and may silently fail on trimmed/normalised bodies**

The switch from `c.body.includes(marker)` to `c.body === body` means the match breaks the moment GitHub's API returns the stored body with any difference from the locally-constructed string — e.g., trailing newline differences, CRLF vs LF, or any future templating change. The prior marker-based approach was robust to those variations. The test constructs `postedBody` from an actual first POST so it round-trips correctly today, but a future change to the comment template (e.g., adding a trailing newline) will silently regress dedup without a failing test. Consider `c.body?.trimEnd() === body.trimEnd()` or anchoring on the marker as a guard and then falling through to a content check, so minor whitespace variance doesn't defeat dedup.

*Suggested fix:*

```suggestion
if (comments.some((c) => c.body?.trimEnd() === body.trimEnd())) {
```

claims.title: Legacy marker removal may silently strip a section that spans across a provider-scoped section
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**Legacy marker removal may silently strip a section that spans across a provider-scoped section**

The legacy strip does a simple `indexOf` + slice: if the PR body happens to contain both the legacy unscoped markers AND an already-injected provider-scoped section whose content lies *between* those legacy markers, the slice `body.slice(legacyStartIdx, legacyEndIdx + ...)` will silently remove the provider-scoped block too. This scenario is possible when: (1) a PR was reviewed before the legacy migration, (2) then the new code ran and appended a provider-scoped section *before* the legacy end marker, and (3) then the migration code runs again. The safest fix is to also remove the provider-scoped section before stripping the legacy range, or to check that `legacyEndIdx > legacyStartIdx` AND that no provider-scoped start marker lies between them before stripping.

claims.title: Legacy-marker strip does not guard against partial matches — wrong slice if only one tag is present
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Legacy-marker strip does not guard against partial matches — wrong slice if only one tag is present**

The migration strip only executes when both `legacyStartIdx !== -1` and `legacyEndIdx !== -1`, which is correct. However, if `LEGACY_PR_SECTION_START` and `LEGACY_PR_SECTION_END` appear in the body in the wrong order (end before start — possible if the body is malformed), `body.slice(0, legacyStartIdx)` correctly takes text before the start tag but `body.slice(legacyEndIdx + ...)` would take text that begins before `legacyStartIdx`, producing duplicated content. This is the same class of ordering bug that affects the existing provider-scoped logic. Low severity because it only fires on an already-malformed body, but worth guarding with `legacyStartIdx < legacyEndIdx`.

*Suggested fix:*

```suggestion
	if (legacyStartIdx !== -1 && legacyEndIdx !== -1 && legacyStartIdx < legacyEndIdx) {
```

claims.title: New test asserts `postedBody` without guarding against `undefined`
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**New test asserts `postedBody` without guarding against `undefined`**

If the POST branch in `octokitFirst.request` is never reached (e.g. because `maybeSubmitReview` returned early), `postedBody` remains `undefined`. The subsequent `expect(postedBody).toContain(...)` passes in Vitest because `undefined` is coerced, but the later `{ data: [{ body: postedBody }] }` feeds `undefined` as a comment body into the second call, making the dedup check compare the real body against `undefined` — which always fails — so the test would incorrectly pass even if dedup is broken. Adding `expect(postedBody).toBeDefined()` before the second `maybeSubmitReview` call makes the failure mode explicit.

*Suggested fix:*

```suggestion
		expect(postedBody).toBeDefined();
		expect(postedBody).toContain(quotaCommentMarker("anthropic"));
```

Full-body match suppresses updated rate-limit warnings posted by a different provider
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Full-body match suppresses updated rate-limit warnings posted by a different provider**

The dedup now matches on exact comment body equality (`c.body === body`). For the rate-limit path, `body` includes the provider-specific marker, so a warning posted under `anthropic` will never suppress one posted under `openai`. That is fine. But within a single provider, if the rate-limit reset window advances between retries, the new `rateLimitResetAt` produces a different body string, so the old comment is no longer a match and the new one is posted alongside it rather than replacing it. The test at line 628 validates this is intentional — "reposts when reset time changed" — but the old comment is never deleted, so a long-lived rate-limited PR accumulates one comment per reset window. This is a pre-existing design gap (the PR doesn't wire up comment editing), but the switch from marker-only to body-exact matching makes it more likely to fire in practice. Worth a follow-up to either delete-then-post or PATCH the existing comment.

**Legacy migration strip is order-sensitive and may silently corrupt the body if the legacy markers appear after new provider-scoped markers**

`injectPRSection` strips the legacy unscoped section before locating the provider-scoped markers. If a body contains both (the exact transitional state described by the docstring — legacy markers still present while provider-scoped sections were already appended by an earlier run of the new code), stripping the legacy block changes `legacyStartIdx`/`legacyEndIdx` offsets but the new `startIdx`/`endIdx` search runs against the already-mutated `body`. **Non-array `existing.data` exits the loop via the `< HAS_EXISTING_COMMENT_PER_PAGE` branch, treating 0 as a short page**

**New assertion only checks `toHaveLength(0)` on POST calls — does not guard against the warning being suppressed by a return before the POST**

The new block at lines 733–739 asserts `posts.toHaveLength(0)`. The comment says this rules out a future change that catches the scan error and posts anyway. But `posts.toHaveLength(0)` is also satisfied if `maybeSubmitReview` returns early before any request is made — the assertion cannot distinguish 'threw before POST' from 'returned normally without POST'. Because `expect(maybeSubmitReview(...)).rejects.toThrow` is still present on line 730, the combination is correct: reject + no POST together do rule out the silenced-error path. This is a documentation nit in the inline comment only, not a code defect.

claims.title: Non-array response warning fires after comments array is already derived — redundant branch
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**Non-array response warning fires after comments array is already derived — redundant branch**

The `!Array.isArray(existing.data)` check at line ~410 (the new `console.warn` block) is placed *after* the ternary that already coerces non-arrays to `[]`. This means the warning is correctly emitted, but the code now traverses two separate branches for the same condition. More importantly, the `comments` variable is set to `[]` unconditionally for non-arrays, and then the `if (!Array.isArray)` block fires again with a `console.warn`. While not a bug per se, the ordering means a reader must trace both branches to understand the behavior. A larger risk: the stop condition `comments.length < HAS_EXISTING_COMMENT_PER_PAGE` immediately after will evaluate to `true` for an empty `comments` array (since `0 < 100`), causing the loop to terminate early — this is the pre-existing "pagination stop condition counts non-array response as a full page" finding, now with a new warning added that makes it *look* like the issue is resolved while the early-exit behavior is unchanged. The warning is purely cosmetic here; the loop still exits.

claims.title: Non-array response log fires before the `comments` variable is used, but `comments` is already set to `[]` — warn fires even on the last page when GitHub returns exactly 0 comments
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Non-array response log fires before the `comments` variable is used, but `comments` is already set to `[]` — warn fires even on the last page when GitHub returns exactly 0 comments**

After the refactor, `comments` is assigned from the ternary on line above, and then the `!Array.isArray` branch fires a `console.warn`. This means a legitimate empty-but-valid array response (`[]`) would NOT trigger the warn (correct), but a genuinely non-array response both assigns `comments = []` and then logs — which is fine. The real issue is sequencing: the warn is emitted *after* `comments` is already set to `[]`, so the fallback behavior already happened silently before the warn fires. This is a minor observability ordering issue rather than a bug, but the warn message says "treating as no comments on this page" when that treatment already occurred one line earlier without any log. The warn should be emitted *before* or *instead of* the silent fallback assignment, or the ternary and the guard should be merged into a single `if/else` block so the intent is clear.

claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**Log message change breaks existing test assertion**

The catch block message was updated to include `owner/repo#pullNumber` and a semicolon-separated continuation, but the previously-open finding (watch.ts:140) noted that the test still asserts the old string. The diff shows the message now reads:

```
`ai-review watch: loadPersistedState unavailable for ${owner}/${repo}#${pullNumber} (${provider}) (KV unavailable); continuing without persisted seeding: ${errMsg(err)}`
```

If the test uses `stringContaining('KV unavailable')` or a similar substring that still appears in the new message, it will pass vacuously. But if it also asserts against the old prefix (`loadPersistedState unavailable for ${provider}`) without the owner/repo prefix, it will now fail. Confirm the corresponding test was updated to match this new format, or the test suite will report a regression.

This is a documentation accuracy issue that should be verified against the actual test that covers it.
